title: Prune
pitch: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access.
about_excerpt: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access. Like Comment Story Updates Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage: trace compromised access, contain its branch and preserve trusted resources. The incident workspace combines credential lineage, human decisions, WebMCP audit activity and exact containment planning. The permanent receipt proves targeted credentials were revoked while the owner and trusted access remained active. Inspiration Revoking a suspicious login does not necessarily secure an account. An attacker who obtains one browser session can create independent ways back in: API keys, connected-application grants, access tokens and secondary sessions. Traditional security pages display these resources as separate lists, leaving the account owner to determine how they are related. A user may revoke the suspicious session, watch it disappear and reasonably believe recovery is complete while an API key created by that session continues working. Prune was inspired by a different mental model: Git-style lineage for account access. Instead of showing only which credentials exist, Prune records where each credential came from. When one login becomes untrusted, the owner and their personal browser agent can investigate and contain everything created from that login without destroying unrelated trusted access. ## What Prune does Prune is embedded access-lineage and account-takeover containment infrastructure for SaaS applications. Every access-producing action records: The organization and account The user and actor session The parent credential The newly created credential The credential type The creation time Redacted request metadata This produces a persistent directed graph: Unfamiliar Windows session ├── Quarterly billing export API key ├── Unfamiliar Data Sync application │ └── Child access token └── Secondary access When the owner identifies an unfamiliar login, Prune opens a recovery incident around that branch. The owner and their personal agent can then: 1. Trace every descendant credential. 2. Inspect usage and security evidence. 3. Classify recognized and unrecognized activity. 4. Preserve trusted devices and operational automation. 5. Compare counterfactual containment strategies. 6. Check lockout and operational risk. 7. Build an immutable recovery plan. 8. Complete independent step-up verification. 9. Approve the exact credential set. 10. Execute one short-lived containment capability. 11. Verify every revoked and preserved resource. 12. Generate a permanent recovery receipt. ## Why WebMCP is essential This workflow crosses sessions, API keys, connected applications, tokens, usage evidence, recovery policy and approval state. Visual browser automation would require an agent to interpret several dangerous settings pages and guess which controls correspond to which credentials. That is too ambiguous for account recovery. A single secure_account tool would also be unsafe because it would hide the investigation and human decisions behind one opaque action. Prune instead exposes 28 granular WebMCP tools covering: - Incident investigation - Session and credential inspection - Descendant tracing - Human classification - Preservation constraints - Counterfactual simulation - Lockout and operational-impact checks - Immutable plan creation - Step-up verification status - Exact-plan approval - One-time containment - Independent outcome verification - Recovery-receipt generation Tool availability changes with the incident’s server-controlled phase. Investigation tools are available first. Planning tools appear only after sufficient evidence has been classified. execute_approved_containment appears only after independent step-up verification and exact human approval. It disappears after its one allowed execution. Retaining an old browser tool reference provides no authority because every request is authenticated, tenant-scoped, schema-validated and checked against current server policy again. ## Human, agent and website collaboration Each participant contributes information the others do not possess. The website knows: - Which credentials exist - Which session created each credential - Their parent-child relationships - Their current status and usage - Which actions policy permits The personal agent can: - Investigate structured evidence - Trace the complete credential branch - Identify unresolved decisions - Ask focused questions - Compare containment alternatives - Explain consequences - Verify the final result The human knows: - Which devices belong to them - Which applications they intentionally connected - Which automation must remain operational - Which activity they recognize - Whether the exact recovery plan should be approved The agent never determines authorization. It never receives passwords, raw API keys, access tokens, verification codes or execution cookies. ## What we built Prune includes: - Independent server-side browser sessions - Secure HTTP-only session cookies - One-time API-key and application-token issuance - Digest-only secret persistence - Connected-application grants and usable child tokens - A normalized PostgreSQL credential graph - Parent-child validation and cycle rejection - Ancestor and descendant traversal - Usage and security-event recording - Manual session-only revocation - Recursive branch containment - Incident creation and evidence collection - Human classifications - Preservation constraints - Three counterfactual containment strategies - Lockout and operational-impact analysis - Canonical immutable plan hashes - Short-lived step-up verification - Exact human approval - One-time execution authority - Idempotent revocation - Post-execution verification - Permanent recovery receipts - Server-sent real-time incident updates - 28 dynamically exposed WebMCP tools - Secret-redacted WebMCP results and audit trails - A complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable - A SaaS integration control plane - Signed event ingestion and replay protection - Instrumentation coverage checks - Confirmed revocation webhooks - A reference TypeScript integration SDK - Automated unit, integration, multi-browser and accessibility tests ## What is real in the demonstration Northstar is a working reference SaaS application protected by Prune. The demonstration creates two genuine independent browser sessions. The unfamiliar browser issues a real API key and connects an application that receives a real child token. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the independently issued API key still returns HTTP 200. This proves why ordinary session revocation is incomplete. video_transcript_excerpt: One compromised session can become several independent ways back into an account, an API key, an application grant, a child token, even another session. This is North Star, a working SaaS application protected by Prune. An unfamiliar browser signs in independently, creates a real API key, then connects an application that receives its own usable token. Prune records each credential, its parent, and the session that created it. The key reaches protected data, 200. The owner revokes only the visible session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the same key still returns 200. Session revocation looks successful. Account recovery was not complete. For agent-assisted recovery, Prune creates a fresh isolated account through the same production services. In ChatGPT, Prune exposes incident-scoped Web MCP tools. This deterministic browser agent evaluation exercises that same registered tool contract against the live deployment. It summarizes the incident, lists the account sessions, traces every descendant, inspects credential usage, and finds remaining access paths. Every call passes through the authenticated application service and appears in Prune's audit trail. No password, API key, or token is returned to the agent. The owner identifies the unfamiliar branch and requires the trusted phone and deployment automation to remain available. Prune records those human decisions, compares containment strategies, and simulates the result without changing account state. Lockout and operational impact are checked before an immutable plan is created. The agent cannot approve its own recommendation. The owner verifies directly with Prune, reviews the exact plan, and approves it. Only then does a short-lived, one-time execution capability appear. Prune executes the approved branch and removes the unfamiliar session, API key, application grant, and child token. The agent independently checks every targeted credential, verifies trusted access, and scans for anything left behind. Both attacker credentials now return 401. The owner session, trusted phone, and deployment automation remain active. Execution authority is consumed. Every outcome is preserved in a permanent recovery receipt. Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage, human-gated containment, and verifiable recovery through Web MCP.
